authority: OWNER-RULINGS.md Ruling 34 §2 (THM-0063: an expired credential, or a non-positive TTL, obtains no signing window; the proxy opens windows at two sites, both through SigningWindow::over; sentence 4 kept and made true of DelegatedSigningCustody::sign_response, which now signs through SigningWindow::over; signature_valid_until deleted)
text:
[[theorem]]
id = "THM-0063"
title = "A signed response never advertises validity its credential does not authorize"
statement = """
`SigningWindow` (in `mcp-re-http-profile`) keeps `expires` private and no constructor accepts
one: every window is derived as the earlier of the configured TTL from `now` and the
credential's own `exp`, with saturating arithmetic so an absurd configured TTL cannot wrap
past it. A credential already past its bound, or a non-positive TTL, obtains no signing
window at all, and with no window nothing is signed. The delegated signing key is
crate-private to its `ActiveDelegatedKey`, and the emitters that read it take a window, so a
signature under a delegated credential cannot advertise any other validity. The proxy opens
windows at two sites — the exchange's opener and a refusal that carries its exchange's
snapshot — and both go through `SigningWindow::over`; every window this deployment signs
under, reply and refusal alike, is opened at one of them, and a refusal signs under the
snapshot its own exchange took.
"""
security_consequence = """
A client cannot be given a receipt asserting validity beyond the moment its credential stops
authorizing signatures — a window the verifier refuses as soon as the credential's own closes,
which the client would learn about only by failing. And a refusal minted late in an exchange
cannot advertise more validity for having been reached by a different path.
"""
direct_consequence_severity = "high"
scope = """
The advertised window, not the signature. It does not establish that a credential existed
(THM-0062) or what the signature covers (THM-0065). Where no valid credential exists the
receipt is UNSIGNED, and what such a receipt may still state is a separate conjunct of this
unit rather than part of this claim.
"""
owner = "proxy.response_signing"
review_requirement = "Owner security-specification review"
supported_by = ["unit://proxy.response_signing", "unit://proxy.delegated_signing_credential", "unit://http_profile.delegated_signing_custody"]
depends_on = ["THM-0062"]

authority: OWNER-RULINGS.md Ruling 34 §3 (THM-0010: proved claim kept; scope states the retained-handle identity across the answer-leg hand-off rests on RetainedContinuation::from_correlation, outside the unit and the proof)
text:
[[theorem]]
id = "THM-0010"
title = "Continuation handles match their retained evidence in slot"
statement = """
An accepted continuation's previous-request and input-required-response handles ARE the two
evidence handles the correlation store retained, compared each in its own slot, and its
request-state handle is the labeled digest of the presented `requestState` under its own
role label.
"""
security_consequence = """
A response-role evidence handle cannot be presented in the request slot, so the positions of
a continuation cannot be permuted. The store retains handles and never a signature base, so a
read of the correlation tier yields no covered `authorization` or `dpop` credential.
"""
direct_consequence_severity = "high"
scope = """
Assumes only that the labeled digest IS A FUNCTION of (label, bytes) — ASM-0023. It does
NOT establish collision-resistant separation between roles; that obligation stays at
boundary.crypto_primitives and is not discharged here. That each retained handle was minted
under its own role label is `RetainedHandles::over`'s, measured in the proxy's
`proxy.continuation_correlation_store`, and not a clause of the proof. That the two handles
`verify` is handed ARE the ones the correlation store retained is the serving path's: the
answer leg hands the peeked handles over through `RetainedContinuation::from_correlation`, the
only constructor of what `verify` consumes. That hand-off lies outside this unit and this
proof; the proof establishes the clauses above for the handles it is given.
"""
owner = "http_profile.continuation_binding"
review_requirement = "Owner security-specification review"
supported_by = ["unit://http_profile.continuation_binding"]
depends_on = []

authority: OWNER-RULINGS.md Ruling 34 §3 (THM-0093: 'the retained open-leg evidence handles are read without being spent'; six stale code comments corrected in the same commit)
text:
[[theorem]]
id = "THM-0093"
title = "An answer leg that needs a continuation does not proceed unbound"
statement = """
Where a request carries a continuation, the retained open-leg evidence handles are read
WITHOUT being spent, and no way they can be absent yields a binding: the dispatcher fails closed rather than
admitting an unbound continuation.

The absences are ATTRIBUTED, not merely detected. A store that does not ANSWER, and a
deployment that holds no correlation capability while this leg needs one, are refused before
admission and named as facts about the DEPLOYMENT. Only the caller-side absences — the request
names no `requestState`, or the store answered and the entry was never opened, has expired, or
was already answered — leave no binding and let the leg be refused as the caller's.

The spend is the store's atomic consume and has four outcomes, because the store's error is
not its negative answer: nothing was at stake, this call spent the approval, the store
answered and there was nothing live to spend, or the store did not answer and whether the
entry is gone cannot be determined by anything downstream.
"""
security_consequence = """
A signed continuation that cannot be bound to a live approval is never admitted, so a second
verified actor cannot complete a human approval round trip that was not its own by presenting
a continuation the deployment cannot check. The read is free, so a request about to be refused
for an unrelated reason leaves a live approval intact — the refusals above the retirement stay
free only because nothing above them spent anything.

A deployment's own missing capability is never reported as the caller's forgery. Without that
conjunct the fail-closed behaviour is still safe and its diagnosis is false: every legitimate
answer leg reaching a deployment that selected no correlation store reads on the wire as a
splice attempt, and a genuine splice attempt is indistinguishable from an ordinary deployment
posture. An operator cannot act on either, and a defender cannot tell them apart.

The four-valued retirement preserves the observed fate of the approval without inventing
certainty: no approval was involved, this exchange spent it, the store answered and there was
nothing live to spend, or its fate is indeterminate. These are four different facts about a
person's decision, and they are carried forward so the exchange-lifecycle authority can derive
the consequence. THM-0093 does not decide retry policy and does not assert that any particular
retry will succeed; what it establishes is that the four facts reach that authority undistorted
rather than collapsed into one another.
"""
direct_consequence_severity = "critical"
scope = """
It is about what a leg may PROCEED on and how a request-time absence is ATTRIBUTED — never
about what the deployment was built or configured with. Which capability the runtime installs
for the plan it was given, and what the startup transcript says about it, is THM-0096's and is
deliberately not restated here. This claim observes its own `ContinuationPlane` state and
consumes no proposition from THM-0096, which is why no edge to it exists: both discuss
absence, and they establish different things.

It says nothing about the continuation binding check itself, which is
`mcp-re-http-profile`'s and is where a bound-but-wrong continuation is caught, and nothing
about what an acknowledged store write durably establishes.

The `Indeterminate` retirement is reported, not resolved. Nothing downstream can find out
whether the entry was consumed, and this claim does not pretend otherwise — what it
establishes is that the outcome is carried as its own case rather than collapsed into one of
the other three.
"""
owner = "proxy.continuation_leg_binding"
review_requirement = "Owner security-specification review"
supported_by = ["unit://proxy.continuation_leg_binding"]
depends_on = ["THM-0087"]

# ADR-MCPRE-059 §28 / issue #746. TWO members, never one theorem.
#
# A single claim over "the SDK" would be a claim about no shipped artefact. The boundary is
# implemented independently per language and the Rust proof establishes nothing about
# either — and the evidence for that is direct and measured: the byte-level parity fixtures
# are GREEN while the implementations diverge behaviourally. Bytes are not behaviour.
#
# Both are root-family members beside THM-0076, which is the Rust member of the same family.
[[theorem]]
id = "THM-0094"
title = "The shipped Python SDK accepts only an answer to its own request"
statement = """
For the shipped Python SDK, an application is not handed, as this call's answer, a response
from another exchange or signer, or one that verified only unbound — and is not led to
repeat a side effect by reading silence as *it did not run*.

The verdict this SDK acts on was computed by the audited core over the exact request bytes
this exchange signed and transmitted; nothing is re-derived or re-serialized for the
verifier, so what THM-0058 and THM-0059 establish about a verdict is established about THIS
transmission. A response is accepted only under a trust picture that was complete at
construction, measured against a RECORDED delegated session rather than a constructed one,
and a request is answerable only inside the window it declared. No request is signed under a
nonce below the 128-bit floor, so a captured answer cannot be aimed at a later call.

A verdict whose outcome is not success reaches the application as a correlated error and
never as a result. What does reach the MCP session is REBUILT from the one member the
verified reply carried plus the session's own id, so a reply carrying a method, or one with
neither result nor error, is refused rather than dispatched. An elicitation pauses a call
rather than ending it: only a terminal verified reply resolves it, and an elicitation with no
handler, a declined one, or one past the continuation budget fails the call closed. A
notification is treated as delivered only against an acknowledgement that verified as bound
to that transmission.

What the application is told about execution is what the receipt said, and nothing else. A
verified receipt carrying execution and retry fields is reported with exactly those fields; a
member the receipt did not carry is not invented for it. A LOCAL failure — a transport
deadline, a cancellation, a local I/O or signing failure — is reported as a local and
ambiguous failure under the SDK's own prefix: never as `not_executed`, never as retry-safe,
and never as a wire code the peer did not send.
"""
security_consequence = """
An application driving MCP through this SDK cannot be handed another exchange's answer, an
answer from a signer this deployment does not trust, or a refusal that verified only unbound
— and cannot be told that an operation did not run when the SDK does not know that.

The last is the one a byte-level fixture cannot reach, and the timeout is where it bites: a
response deadline is the condition under which this SDK knows LEAST about whether the call
ran, so a synthesized `not_executed` or retry-safe verdict there is exactly what makes a
caller repeat a tool call that already executed. Parity fixtures pin what this SDK EMITS;
whether it invents an execution fact for a receipt that stated nothing is behaviour, and the
two SDKs have diverged there before.
"""
direct_consequence_severity = "critical"
scope = """
It is one MEMBER of a root family, not the family. THM-0076 is the Rust member and THM-0095
the TypeScript one; none of the three establishes anything about the others, and a green
parity fixture is not a substitute — it compares bytes, and every divergence this family
exists for is behavioural.

THE CORRELATION CLAIM WAS NARROWED ON 2026-09-18, and the narrowing makes the promise
better supported rather than smaller. The statement used to say that a reply "binding to
nothing outstanding, arriving late, or repeating one already answered is refused rather than
delivered". Measured against `_exchange`, two of those three are unreachable: the correlation
id handed to `CorrelationStore.take()` is the one `record()` returned three statements
earlier in the same loop iteration, and MCP-RE is one signed POST per request, so there is no
inbox and no lookup by any value a peer controls. Those two refusals are real properties of
`CorrelationStore` AS A VALUE, exercised at its own API, and they are stated there. What
binds a reply to its request on the shipped path is the audited core over the bytes this
exchange signed — which is why that is now the statement's first sentence and why
THM-0058/THM-0059 are now premises instead of being silently relied on. The system promise is
unchanged; what changed is that it names the mechanism that keeps it.

THE PyO3 BINDING IS NOT COVERED. `sdk/python/src/lib.rs` builds the pinned root resolver, the
delegation policy and the revocation list, calls the core, and projects the core's verdict
into the object this claim's execution-honesty leaf reports verbatim. It is in no unit's
paths, so it is outside every fingerprint and outside every proposition, and it holds no
tests of its own. This claim therefore ASSUMES the projection is faithful rather than
establishing it — recorded as a review obligation, not waved past. Until it is discharged,
the closure below establishes what the Python layer does with a verdict, not that the verdict
object says what the core decided.

CONCURRENCY AND THROUGHPUT ARE OUTSIDE IT. The exchange bound is a resource ceiling, and a
difference from the TypeScript member there changes nothing about authenticity, correlation
or execution. Deadline behaviour enters only where a timeout changes the client's conclusion
about whether the remote side may have executed.

THE RESPONSE READ BOUND IS OUTSIDE IT, AND ITS WORST CASE IS STATED RATHER THAN ROUNDED OFF.
`read1` prevents a fill-to read from suppressing the aggregate-deadline check across multiple
underlying reads: once the deadline has passed, no NEW underlying read is begun. An
underlying read already in progress may straddle the deadline, and the existing per-recv
timeout bounds that final stall. So the cap is the aggregate deadline plus at most one
per-recv timeout — at most twice `timeout` under the single value a deployment sets — and NOT
an exact wall-clock bound. It is measured against a real `http.client.HTTPResponse` fed by a
real socket, both while trickling and while silent, never against a fake with short-read
semantics the production reader lacks. But the bound itself is AVAILABILITY: remove it and a
trickling peer holds a worker, which hands the application no wrong answer. What this claim
takes from the deadline is only honesty — the deadline fails the exchange as a LOCAL
condition and manufactures no execution or retry fact — and that is
`sdk_python.local_failure_provenance`'s proposition, not the bound's. The bound keeps its own
unit at its own severity.

WHAT A CALLER DOES NEXT IS OUTSIDE THIS ROOT. This claim says nothing about an application's
own retry policy, its outer timeouts, or what it concludes from a local failure; it says only
that the SDK does not hand it a peer verdict or an execution fact the peer never gave. Retry
policy outside this adapter is not this adapter's proposition.

REQUEST-SIDE ATTRIBUTION IS OUTSIDE IT. Which identity may sign, and under which custody
class, is `sdk_python.signer_policy`; which authorization artefacts a request is bound to is
`sdk_python.authorization_binding`. Remove either and the answer the application receives
still binds to the request that was sent, which is why neither is in this closure.

THE SUPPORTED RUNTIME SET IS PART OF THE CLAIM. "The shipped Python SDK" means the package
as it runs on the interpreters it declares support for, and that is a measured set rather
than an inference from one machine: `requires-python = ">=3.14.5,<3.15"`, and the battery
runs on every minor in that range at the exact patch versions `toolchains.lock.toml`
`[python].interpreters` pins. The runtime identity is inside each unit's fingerprint, so
changing an interpreter drops the standing evidence instead of silently carrying it; a
minor outside the range is outside this claim; and `scripts/python_runtime_gate.py`
refuses a support claim wider than the measured set. It matters here specifically because
the read bound above rests on stdlib `read1` behaviour, which is a per-minor fact.

THE SET WAS NARROWED ON 2026-09-05, from CPython 3.10-3.14 to 3.14 alone, and the claim is
smaller for it. This is a WITHDRAWAL of support, not a correction: the earlier range was
inherited from the upstream MCP SDK's own floor and cost a battery on five interpreters to
hold. Anything running 3.10 through 3.13 is now outside this claim entirely — not weakly
covered, not covered by inference from an adjacent minor. The floor's patch component is
part of the proposition and not a formality: 3.14.0 through 3.14.4 ship the incremental
cycle collector CPython reverted in 3.14.5, so they are outside the claim as surely as
3.13 is.

It says nothing about the transport below it, nothing about the proxy's own guarantees, and
nothing about an application that bypasses this adapter.
"""
owner = "sdk_python.exchange_binding"
review_requirement = "Owner security-specification review"
# ADR-MCPRE-068 Phase 1. Ten leaves, each one proposition with one owner and one carrier,
# and the decomposition's own falsifier is recorded in the packet: removing any one of the
# ten makes the root's consequence reachable, and the inverse question returned the three
# units deliberately left outside this closure.
supported_by = [
  "unit://sdk_python.exchange_binding",
  "unit://sdk_python.verdict_delivery",
  "unit://sdk_python.execution_report",
  "unit://sdk_python.local_failure_provenance",
  "unit://sdk_python.reply_envelope",
  "unit://sdk_python.continuation_drive",
  "unit://sdk_python.correlation_lifecycle",
  "unit://sdk_python.nonce_floor",
  "unit://sdk_python.notification_delivery",
  "unit://sdk_python.trust_anchor_completeness",
]
# `depends_on` was EMPTY, and that was false. The Python SDK's whole cryptographic argument
# is the audited core's: `verify_delegated_response` decides binding, trust, revocation,
# epoch and audience; `DelegationPolicy` clamps the skew; `ExecutionContract` and
# `continuation_state` decide what a receipt stated and whether a reply is terminal. Those
# are MCP-RE's own registered units, not an external boundary, and a root that did not name
# them read as a self-contained claim over five Python files.
#
# THM-0126 is deliberately NOT here. It is `mcp-re-client-proxy`'s own outcome resolution,
# and the PyO3 binding derives the same fact independently rather than consuming it — which
# is a duplicated representation recorded as Phase-2 work, not an edge this argument uses.
# CORRECTED under the ADR-MCPRE-068 Phase-1 campaign ruling of 2026-09-18, which authorizes
# correcting a statement decomposition shows overstates or misdescribes what production
# establishes, provided the accepted promise is not weakened, removed or materially expanded.
# Six corrections, C1-C6, recorded old->new in
# `verification/claim-corrections/THM-0094-2026-09-18.json` with the reason from the
# decomposition, and argued in `packets/thm-0094-consequence-decomposition-2026-09-18.md` §10.
#
# `depends_on` WAS EMPTY AND THAT WAS FALSE: the SDK's whole cryptographic argument is
# `mcp_re_client_core`'s. THM-0126 is deliberately excluded — the PyO3 binding derives that
# fact independently rather than consuming it, which is the packet's P2-D.
depends_on = ["THM-0058", "THM-0059", "THM-0060", "THM-0061"]

authority: OWNER-RULINGS.md Ruling 34 §3 (THM-0104: the accept loop observes the shutdown signal within one accept-poll interval and exits before the drain begins; a connection accepted inside that interval is counted and drained like any other; no accept-loop redesign)
text:
[[theorem]]
id = "THM-0104"
title = "Shutdown stops admission and bounds the wait on admitted work; what the drain leaves behind it never resumes"
statement = """
For one core of the async serving path, from the moment a shutdown is signalled:

ADMISSION STOPS. The accept loop observes the shutdown signal within one accept-poll interval
and exits before the drain begins; a connection accepted inside that interval is counted and
drained like any other. The drain signal puts every connection that exists into graceful
shutdown: it finishes the requests it has, writes their responses, and admits no further
request on it, keep-alive or multiplexed alike.

ADMITTED WORK IS COUNTED UNTIL ITS CONNECTION ENDS. A connection is OPEN from an RAII guard
taken at accept, before its TLS handshake, until its connection task ends. The guard's
construction is the only increment and its `Drop` the only decrement, so a connection cannot
be served without being counted, nor counted after it has finished. The task lives until the
HTTP layer has finished the connection, which is after the last response it started has been
written and flushed, so the count is a count of connections not yet finished — never of
requests not yet started, and never of requests whose handler has merely returned. A reply
still being written holds the count above zero.

THE DRAIN WAITS ON THAT COUNT, BOUNDED. It signals the drain, then polls while the count is
non-zero and returns when the count reaches zero OR the grace deadline passes, whichever comes
first. A grace that cannot be turned into an instant makes the drain decline to start rather
than park process exit behind a deadline it cannot enforce.

WHAT THE GRACE LEAVES BEHIND MAY BE CANCELLED. When the drain returns, the core's runtime is
dropped and a task still suspended at an await point is cancelled there. That await point may
be anywhere a connection's processing suspends, INCLUDING INSIDE THE HANDLER and INSIDE THE
WRITE OF A REPLY: a reply the grace cut off is the grace's doing and nothing before it.

CANCELLATION IS TERMINAL. A task cancelled by the runtime drop is never polled again: it does
not enter the handler afterwards, and it does not resume inside it. Once `serve` returns, no
admitted request makes further progress — which is the fact teardown's second phase relies on
when it drops the trust, signing and TLS planes.
"""
security_consequence = """
An operator draining a replica — a rolling deploy, a scale-down, a node drain — gets two
facts, and must not be sold a third.

The two: nothing new is admitted once the accept loop has observed the signal, and no
admitted request executes, or
resumes executing, after `serve` returns, so the planes are dismantled behind work that has
provably stopped rather than work assumed to have stopped. Within the grace, a reply a
connection had started is delivered rather than cut off by the runtime drop.

The third, which this mechanism does NOT provide: that a request cancelled at grace expiry
had not already executed. The in-flight count does not distinguish a request stalled in its
body read from one suspended inside the handler, so once the grace expires the drain cannot
say on which side of the exchange's execution threshold the abandoned work sat.

Whether a client may safely retry an abandoned request is therefore decided by the exchange
state and retry authorities, on the evidence THOSE authorities hold about how far the exchange
progressed — never by the drain counter. A deployment wanting zero-abandoned drain in fact
rather than in bound configures `drain_grace >= request_deadline`; that is a configuration
relation resting on the request deadline's own enforcement, and is not claimed here.
"""
direct_consequence_severity = "medium"
scope = """
WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED, in terms, because an earlier statement of this theorem claimed all three
and was corrected by owner ruling on 2026-09-06: that a request which reached the handler runs
to completion and is answered; that every admitted request ends answered or never executed;
that retry of an abandoned request is safe because the handler was never entered. The
connection guard spans handshake, body read, handler and response writing alike, and the drain
exits on the grace as readily as on the count, so runtime teardown after grace expiry can cancel a task suspended
INSIDE `handler(..).await`. The battery's
`a_request_abandoned_by_the_grace_never_reaches_the_handler` exercises a request stalled in its
BODY READ; it establishes that cancellation is terminal for a task that had not yet reached the
handler, not that every abandoned task is such a task.

NOTHING HERE BOUNDS HOW LONG TEARDOWN TAKES. That an idle drain returns promptly, that a
saturated drain finishes within a few seconds, and that a stuck request cannot delay exit much
past the grace are WALL-CLOCK MEASUREMENTS taken on the box that ran them — real controls
(`idle_drain_returns_promptly`, `stuck_request_cannot_delay_exit_past_grace`, and the tail
assertions of the two zero-abandoned controls), part of the battery this unit's evidence rests
on, but not conjuncts of this claim. A red from one of them is a statement about the machine,
not about the property. The bounded-exit guarantee an operator configures (`drain_grace` under
a Kubernetes termination grace period) is that timing property and is therefore not claimed
here either.

ONE core, and the async path. The per-core fleet inherits the mechanism because each core's
`serve` drains before its worker thread joins, but that composition is not stated. The blocking
mTLS harness is not an MCP-RE serving path and is out of scope.

The cancellation half is STRUCTURAL — a task suspended at an await point when its runtime is
dropped is not polled again — and has no deletable check, so it carries no probe; what a probe
can reach is the drain's wait and the guard that makes the count move. The three non-UTF-8
header controls sharing this test binary belong to a boundary-refusal authority that has no
owner, and are not evidence for anything here.

Outside every root's closure, deliberately and for the same reason as THM-0012: no root's
dispatch or response claim rests on what shutdown does to work already admitted. Executable,
class V0, measured under the `async_serve` feature lane named by the owning unit.
"""
owner = "proxy.serving_drain"
review_requirement = "Owner security-specification review"
supported_by = ["unit://proxy.serving_drain"]
depends_on = []

authority: OWNER-RULINGS.md Ruling 34 §3 (THM-0133: D1 conditional on a configured shared trust-epoch counter, a single-replica deployment without one minting under the bare base label; D2 names `mcp-re-proxy trust-epoch advance` with the forward-only repair and generation semantics; raw INCR not a supported advance; ASM-0071 and the startup banner corrected in the same pass)
text:
[[theorem]]
id = "THM-0133"
title = "With a shared trust-epoch counter configured, the delegated-signing plane mints only under the label its own read names, and never under a regressed one"
statement = """
When a shared trust-epoch counter is configured (`--trust-epoch-redis-url`), the label the
delegated-signing plane hands its rotor is `<base>#<counter>`, where `counter` is the value
this replica's most recent successful read of the shared counter returned. It is then never
the bare base label and never relative to a value this process read earlier, so every replica
whose read returns the same value derives the same label, whenever it started. A legal
deployment with no shared counter configured mints under the bare base label, which never
advances.

A read that fails yields no label. A read that returns a counter below the highest this
process has read, or no counter at all, also yields no label: the regression is refused, not
adopted. The replica then repairs FORWARD: it moves the shared counter to one past its
high-water mark in one atomic store step that writes only while the counter is absent or below
that mark — so a second replica repairing from the same mark writes nothing and an advance
above the mark is never overwritten — and mints again once a read is at or above the mark. A
read whose counter is at the mark but whose advance generation this replica has not seen is a
fresh advance landing on an acknowledged label: it is refused and repaired forward the same
way, and the generation is recorded only once the counter is past the mark. No label means
nothing is minted.
"""
security_consequence = """
The operator's supported advance is `mcp-re-proxy trust-epoch advance`, which commits the
incremented counter together with a fresh generation drawn from the OS in one server-side step.
It is a kill switch only if what the plane mints follows the counter. A label taken from a
per-process baseline let a replica that restarted after an advance adopt the advanced value as
its own starting point and keep minting under an epoch the verifiers still accepted; a label
adopted from a regressed read, or from a counter a rollback returned to a value already minted
under, would re-mint under an epoch the verifiers have already stopped accepting, resurrecting
the credentials the advance retired. Both are excluded here: every advance a replica reads ends
strictly beyond that replica's mark, and a counter that cannot be read stops issuance rather
than letting it continue under a label nobody checked. A raw `INCR` on the key moves only the
number and is not a supported advance.
"""
direct_consequence_severity = "high"
scope = """
LOCAL TO ONE REPLICA. This states what the plane does with the value its read returned. That the
read returns the advanced value after an operator's advance on another connection is ASM-0071,
the store's fact and not MCP-RE's; "an advance moves every replica to the next label" is this
claim composed with that premise, and is no stronger than the premise. Across a restart the
high-water mark is gone and the shared counter is the only authority: a replica that starts while
the store is regressed mints under the regressed label until a live peer's repair raises the
counter, and a fleet that restarts entirely while the store is regressed has no mark left to
repair toward.

It says nothing about credentials already issued under an earlier label: no verifier reads the
counter, so a credential minted before the advance stays verifiable until the verifiers' accepted
epochs are changed. Nothing about the startup refusal when the first read fails, which
`proxy.signing_plane_epoch_read_refusal` measures, nor about when the rotation loop re-reads the
counter. And no ordering between this plane's observation of an advance and the request-trust
cache's flush on the same counter (THM-0097's scope disclaims it from the other side).
"""
owner = "proxy.delegated_epoch_label"
review_requirement = "Owner security-specification review"
supported_by = ["unit://proxy.delegated_epoch_label"]
depends_on = []

authority: OWNER-RULINGS.md Ruling 34 §4 (THM-0024: the consequence describes the current surface — only URI and DNS SANs are identity fields — and no longer names the deleted Common-Name downgrade path)
text:
[[theorem]]
id = "THM-0024"
title = "Certificate identity interpretation reads the configured field and refuses rather than falling back"
statement = """
If interpreting certificate-chain evidence under an identity-selection policy returns Ok,
then: the returned source equals the field the policy configures; the returned value is the
PeerIdentityValue interpretation of the FIRST value the leaf presents in that field; and the
value satisfies THM-0023.

If it returns Err, no other field and no later value of the configured field was read. The
five refusals are distinguishable: no leaf was presented, the leaf could not be interpreted
as a certificate, the representation carrying the configured field could not be interpreted,
the configured field was absent, or the configured field's first value was not a well-formed
identity — the last carrying which value rule it broke. Present-but-uninterpretable is never
reported as absent, and the refusal names the first rule that failed under the precedence
readability -> presence -> identity-value validity.

Interpretation is total and deterministic over the interpreted field set and the policy.
"""
security_consequence = """
An issuer or peer cannot choose which identity the proxy binds to by controlling a field
the deployment did not configure, and cannot choose it by making the authoritative value
unusable: neither a present DNS SAN under a URI-SAN policy nor a valid second URI SAN
behind a malformed first one is ever read. Only URI and DNS SANs are identity fields: the
subject Common Name is not one, no policy selects it, and the adapter does not read it.
"""
direct_consequence_severity = "critical"
scope = """
It establishes IDENTITY EVIDENCE and nothing above it. It does not establish that the
certificate chain is trusted, that it is unrevoked, that it is fresh, that the peer is
authenticated, that the relationship is admitted, that any action is authorized, or that a
channel to that peer exists. Holding the product is not a weaker form of any of those, and
none of them may be inferred from it.

The claim divides at the parser boundary. The selector half is over an interpreted field
set — an ordinary Rust value — and is what the battery and any future proof reach. That the
field set faithfully reports what the DER encodes is ASM-0030, an assumed foreign
dependency, NOT part of this claim: a wrong parser yields a faithful interpretation of the
wrong fields and this theorem still holds.

It characterizes values successfully returned by the interpretation operation. It says
nothing about arbitrary possession of a CertificatePeerIdentityEvidence value, whose
construction closure is the module boundary rather than a proved postcondition.

"First value" is a property of the presented order. The claim assumes the field set
preserves that order and does not establish it of any other producer.

The refusals are distinguishable but not equally consequential: every one of them refuses,
so nothing is admitted on any of them. What the distinction establishes is which fact a
refusal RECORDS — an operator, an audit trail and a test can tell a peer that presented
nothing from one whose issuer minted a broken field. It is a claim about faithful reporting,
not about admission.
"""
owner = "proxy.certificate_identity"
review_requirement = "Owner security-specification review"
# TWO units. `proxy.certificate_identity` establishes what the interpreter DECIDES — the
# configured field, no fallback, every refusal named. `proxy.certificate_identity_authority_boundary`
# establishes that the value/source PAIRING happens only inside the communication-assurance
# authority, which is what makes the `source` a provenance report rather than a label any
# module could attach.
supported_by = [
  "unit://proxy.certificate_identity",
  "unit://proxy.certificate_identity_authority_boundary",
  "unit://proxy.certificate_identity_refusal_vocabulary",
]
depends_on = ["THM-0023"]

authority: OWNER-RULINGS.md Ruling 34 §4 (THM-0131 extended with the established CRL controls: authentication against the configured client CA keys (53aa4f78) and reload succession refusing a dropped issuer or a regressed or reused crlNumber (69fe1c13); no dependents)
text:
[[theorem]]
id = "THM-0131"
title = "The client-revocation posture states what this replica is enforcing now"
statement = """
A set of client CRLs is installable only when every one of them is inside its own
`nextUpdate` window and states one at all. That is a property of the value, not of a call
site: the evidence type has a single constructor and the constructor performs the
classification, so startup and the reload worker run one gate rather than two that agree. The
same constructor authenticates every CRL against the configured client CA keys, so a CRL no
configured CA signed has no inhabitant; and a reload installs a set only when it succeeds the
set in force — no issuer dropped, no crlNumber regressed or reused with other bytes.

Each successful reload republishes the evidence it installed, so the posture names the CRLs
in force rather than the ones read at boot. And a replica whose reload worker has died, or
whose plane has retired, retracts the cadence it advertised: the maintenance verdict is
latched, and no later reload can clear it.
"""
security_consequence = """
An operator reading this replica's revocation posture is reading what it is doing. Three
specific misreadings are closed:

* a CRL that startup refuses to boot on could be installed by a reload and reported as
  "new verifier is live", after which — expiration being enforced — every new handshake
  against that issuer failed closed, an outage the transcript attributed to success;
* after any successful reload the posture reported the boot digest and window forever, so
  the CRL an operator checked against the one they published was not the one being
  enforced;
* a panicked reload worker printed a FATAL line and changed nothing, so the deployment went
  on advertising "hot-reload enabled (every Ns)" while nothing re-read the files. The
  self-bounding argument that licenses the weaker treatment covers the rustls VERIFIER; it
  does not cover the per-request index, whose whole purpose is that a peer added to a
  reloaded CRL stops being served on the connection it already holds, and its bound is a
  CRL validity period rather than the cadence the startup line promised.

The latch's two flags are the security content of the third: one flag would let a straggler
reload landing after the worker died report the cadence as kept.
"""
direct_consequence_severity = "medium"
scope = """
V0: a test battery over the evidence constructor, the maintenance algebra and the
retraction, plus the plane's own retirement path.

It is a claim about what the deployment SAYS and about what may be installed. It is NOT a
fail-closed: a dead reload worker does not refuse handshakes, deliberately, because the
verifier does self-bound once the last-good CRL passes its own `nextUpdate` and refusing
would convert a bounded staleness into an immediate outage. What is claimed is that the
advertised property is withdrawn, not that the exposure is zero.

It says nothing about whether a revoked peer is refused — that is THM-0054's handshake half
and the per-request index beside it — and nothing about the CRLs being the right CRLs,
which is an operator decision.

The retraction reaches an operator through stderr. Whether a log pipeline consumes it is
outside this repository, and no claim here rests on its doing so.
"""
owner = "proxy.client_revocation_currency"
review_requirement = "Owner security-specification review"
supported_by = ["unit://proxy.client_revocation_currency", "unit://proxy.client_crl_next_update_gate", "unit://proxy.retired_plane_cadence_retraction", "unit://proxy.client_crl_reload_republish"]
depends_on = ["THM-0054"]

authority: OWNER-RULINGS.md Ruling 34 §3 (ASM-0071 wording corrected with THM-0133: the operator's advance is `mcp-re-proxy trust-epoch advance`, which commits counter and generation in one step, so the premise is stated over the (counter, generation) pair the plane reads; no raw INCR)
text:
[[assumption]]
id = "ASM-0071"
description = "A read of the trust-epoch key and its generation over the delegated-signing plane's own connection, issued after an operator's `mcp-re-proxy trust-epoch advance` on that key was acknowledged, returns a counter and generation different, as a pair, from every pair that plane read before the advance."
justification = """
The sibling of ASM-0044, for the consumer ASM-0044 excludes by name. `DelegatedEpochWatch` reads
the same shared counter over its own connection and mints under `<base>#<counter>` for whatever
the read returned (THM-0133), and the plane tells the operator at startup that
`mcp-re-proxy trust-epoch advance` moves every replica to the next label. That sentence is
THM-0133 composed with this premise: the advance — the incremented counter and a fresh generation,
committed in one server-side step — is issued on a connection this replica does not hold, and what a later `GET` on the plane's
connection returns is decided by the store's replication and routing, not by anything here.

Narrow on purpose, exactly as ASM-0044 is: not "Redis is correct", not durability of the counter,
not ordering between replicas, and not that every replica observes the advance at the same time
— only that an acknowledged write becomes visible to a subsequent read on another connection. A
read that returns the OLD value is the case excluded here, and the one that would keep this
replica minting under a label the operator meant to retire. A read that FAILS, or returns a LOWER
value, is outside the premise and handled locally: no label, so nothing is minted.

It is a separate entry rather than a widening of ASM-0044 because the two consumers make
different local decisions with the value — a flush there, a refusal here — and a premise about
what one plane's read means must not be read as an ordering between the two planes'
observations, which nothing in the tree establishes.

It stops being acceptable if the epoch key is served from a read replica that can lag the
primary, if the deployment routes the plane's connection to a different primary than the
operator's, or if the key can be evicted or restored to an older value without that reading as
absence or regression at the reader.
"""
scope = ["unit://proxy.delegated_epoch_label", "boundary://boundary.shared_state_store"]
owner = "mats@sundvall.name"
introduced_by = "owner-signature:asm-delegated-epoch-label-store-premise (r12, 5fc98328eee54d1a)"
review_requirement = "Owner review; any change to the delegated plane's epoch reader, to the label it derives, or to the store topology the deployment documentation admits for the epoch key."
premise_class = "external-boundary"
boundary_owner = """
The shared-state store, across its read-your-acknowledged-writes ordering for the trust-epoch key
as the delegated-signing plane reads it, under the store topology the deployment documentation
admits for that key.
"""
affected_contracts = []
tool_specific_mechanism = "foreign-dependency"

authority: OWNER-RULINGS.md Ruling 34 §5 (ASM-0038: authority-reference correction; its justification's cross-reference to ASM-0030 no longer names the subject Common Name, deleted under Ruling 31.1)
reference_correction: supporting/reference description corrected because the Common-Name authority was deleted (f354921c, Ruling 31.1)
text:
[[assumption]]
id = "ASM-0038"
description = "The X.509 parser faithfully reports a certificate's validity instants, the DER encodings of its issuer and subject `Name`, and its serial number."
justification = """
`x509_parser` is a foreign ASN.1/X.509 implementation, and `credential_currency/x509_adapter`
is the one place the currency authority meets it. The adapter reads and decides nothing: it
reports `notBefore`, `notAfter`, `issuer.as_raw()`, `raw_serial()`, and whether the issuer
`Name` encoding equals the subject `Name` encoding.

This is NOT ASM-0030. That assumption is about identity fields — URI and DNS SANs and
their presentation order — and about the authority that decides
WHO a peer is. Currency decides something else from a different field set: whether a
credential is still acceptable at a named instant. Neither premise implies the other, and
the earlier attempt to let ASM-0030 stand for both is what this entry replaces.

The consequences of the two halves differ, and both are stated rather than averaged:

  * The VALIDITY INSTANTS bound the claim. A parser reporting the wrong window yields a
    faithful evaluation of the wrong window — a wrong currency verdict, not an unsound
    proof — which is exactly why it is recorded.
  * The `Name` ENCODINGS and the SERIAL are lookup keys into a CRL index. A parser that
    reported another certificate's issuer or serial would look up another certificate's
    revocation standing, so a failure here can make a revoked credential read as current.
    That is a stronger consequence than the identity case and is not softened here.

Equality of the two `Name` encodings is trusted only as a REPORTED SHAPE. What a self-issued
certificate is exempt from is `evaluation`'s decision, not the parser's, and this premise
does not reach it.

It is not proved here: an ASN.1 decoder is a far larger verification target than the
authority that consumes it, and attempting it would put the proof boundary in the wrong
place.

It stops being acceptable if the currency authority acquires a second certificate parser
whose reported fields must agree with this one's, if it begins branching on the parser's
error kinds (today every parse failure is one refusal), or if revocation lookup moves to a
key this premise does not name.
"""
scope = ["unit://proxy.credential_currency", "boundary://boundary.x509"]
owner = "mats@sundvall.name"
introduced_by = "Owner completeness ruling A, 2026-08-31"
review_requirement = "Owner review; any change to the credential-currency X.509 adapter, to its parser dependency, or to the field set revocation lookup is keyed by."
premise_class = "external-boundary"
boundary_owner = """
The pinned `x509_parser` crate, across its certificate decoding API: it reports validity instants, the DER encodings of issuer and subject `Name`, and the serial number faithfully — the field set revocation lookup is keyed by.
"""
affected_contracts = []
tool_specific_mechanism = "foreign-dependency"

authority: OWNER-RULINGS.md Ruling 34 §5 (ASM-0032: authority-reference correction; its justification's cross-reference to ASM-0030 no longer names the subject Common Name, deleted under Ruling 31.1)
reference_correction: supporting/reference description corrected because the Common-Name authority was deleted (f354921c, Ruling 31.1)
text:
[[assumption]]
id = "ASM-0032"
description = "The X.509 certificate parser faithfully reports the leaf certificate's SubjectPublicKeyInfo bytes."
justification = """
The credential adapter parses the leaf with `X509Certificate::from_der` and takes
`certificate.public_key().raw` as the SubjectPublicKeyInfo the credential presented. Both
halves are foreign: that the bytes parse as a certificate at all, and that the SPKI slice
reported is the one the certificate actually carries.

This premise is NOT covered by the two assumptions already registered, and the distinction
matters because their containments differ:

  * ASM-0030 covers the identity-field reporting of Slice 1 — URI and DNS SANs, and their
    presentation order. It says nothing about the public key.
  * ASM-0031 covers the SubjectPublicKeyInfo parser used ONLY after canonical matching has
    already failed, and only to classify a refusal. It is contained to reporting by
    construction, and that containment is exactly what does not apply here: this premise
    sits on the ACCEPTING path, between certificate bytes and the bytes handed to
    `Ed25519PublicKeyValue::interpret_rfc8410_spki`.

A parser that reported another certificate's SPKI, or a slice that is not the SPKI, would
let correspondence hold against a key the credential does not present — so unlike ASM-0031
this assumption can affect acceptance, and it is registered rather than folded into a
neighbouring one for that reason.

It is contained to the credential half of the correspondence relation. The signer half —
that the exported SPKI names the key that will actually sign — is a different premise
crossing a different boundary, and is ASM-0039.

It is not proved here: an X.509 decoder is a far larger verification target than the
authority consuming it, and attempting it would put the proof boundary in the wrong place.

It stops being acceptable if the credential adapter ever re-encodes the SPKI rather than
taking the parser's bytes verbatim — a re-encoding would make this code a second opinion on
what the credential says — or if a second certificate parser is introduced whose reported
SPKI must agree with this one's.
"""
scope = ["unit://proxy.credential_key_correspondence", "boundary://boundary.x509"]
owner = "mats@sundvall.name"
introduced_by = "ADR-MCPRE-063 Slice 2"
review_requirement = "Owner review; any change to the credential adapter's certificate parsing or its parser dependency."
premise_class = "external-boundary"
boundary_owner = """
The pinned `x509_parser` crate, across its certificate decoding API: it reports the leaf certificate's SubjectPublicKeyInfo bytes faithfully.
"""
affected_contracts = []
tool_specific_mechanism = "foreign-dependency"
